::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will explore a dataset before modelling it. You will also learn five rules that turn a chart people have to decode into one they understand at a glance, each shown as a before-and-after pair.
:::

## Look before you model

Exploratory data analysis (EDA) is the step where you find out what the data really is, before you ask it to answer anything. Four questions come first, and the summary table below answers all of them for the rainfall data used in Chapter [-@sec-dataviz]:

1. How much data is there, and how much is missing?
2. What is the typical value, and how wide is the spread?
3. Are there values that cannot be right?
4. Does the data have a rhythm (a season, a trend) that must be removed before comparing?

The table already shows something a mean would hide. In Kupang and Makassar the mean month is far above the median month. A few very wet months pull the mean up, and most months are much drier than the average suggests.

## Five rules for graphs

Each rule is one pair of panels: on the left the graph that most reports contain, on the right a better one. Look at how small the extra effort is.

1. **Show the distribution, not only the average.** A bar of means hides how much individual years differ.
2. **Do not average the variation away.** No real year looks like the average year. Show the range.
3. **Keep axes honest.** A bar's length is its message. Cutting the axis turns a small gap into a big one.
4. **Enough, not too much.** Six colours and a legend make the reader work. Grey context and one highlighted line tell a story.
5. **Make the graph explain itself.** A title that states the finding, units on every axis, the data source, and labels on the points that matter.

{{< include _snippets/ch38_eda_graphs.qmd >}}

## Question 4 in practice: season, trend and remainder

The fourth question, whether the data has a rhythm, deserves a tool of its own. **STL** (seasonal-trend decomposition using LOESS) splits a series into three parts that add back up to it: a *season* that repeats every year, a *trend* that moves slowly, and a *remainder* that is everything else. Rainfall is strongly skewed, so the figure decomposes its square root, which keeps the wettest months from dominating.

For Kupang, the season and trend together explain 85 % of the month-to-month variation. That is the first finding: most of what happens in a rainfall series is the calendar. The trend wanders between dry and wet spells of several years, with no steady rise or fall. The remainder is where the interesting months live. The three largest are November 2021 and November 2022, both far wetter than the season predicts, and February 2024, far drier. The first two fall in the long La Niña of 2020-2023, the last in the El Niño of 2023-24. The decomposition does not know about ENSO; it only isolates the months that need an explanation. That is what exploration is for.

## Relationships: does the Pacific decide the dry season?

A correlation matrix (above) shows which cities move together. A more useful question asks what moves them. The Niño 3.4 index, the sea-surface temperature anomaly in the central Pacific published monthly by NOAA, is the standard measure of El Niño (warm) and La Niña (cold).

Comparing July-October rainfall with the Niño 3.4 anomaly over the same months, 1991-2024, gives a negative rank correlation in all six cities, from -0.60 in Padang to -0.82 in Makassar. In the ten El Niño years (anomaly at least +0.5 °C), the median July-October rainfall was 31 % below normal in Padang and Pontianak, and 66-68 % below normal in Jakarta and Makassar. In the six La Niña years it was above normal everywhere. The small multiples make the pattern visible at once because every panel shares the same axes; with separate axes the reader would compare tick labels instead of points.

Three cautions keep this honest. First, the comparison is between the same months, so it describes association, not a forecast; a forecast would use the Pacific in May or June. Second, percentages of a small number are large: Kupang's dry season is so dry that one wet La Niña year can read as +200 %, which is why the table reports medians. Third, 34 years hold only ten El Niño and six La Niña years. The Spearman correlations are very unlikely to be chance (p < 0.001 everywhere), but the El Niño and La Niña medians rest on few years each.

## Question 3 in practice: values that cannot be right

Satellite data has its own impossible values, and the best place to learn to see them is a single pixel over a single year. The figure shows every daytime land surface temperature that MODIS Terra recorded for one pixel in central Bandung in 2023: 155 days out of 365, because the rest were cloudy.

The product carries a quality flag for every value. In the humid tropics almost every value is "produced, check the other flags", so the useful part of the flag is the estimated error: 135 of the 155 days (87 %) have an estimated error of 2 K or less. A second, independent check comes from the data itself: compare each day with the median of the 15 days around it, scale by the median absolute deviation, and call anything more than three robust standard deviations away an outlier. Six days fail that test, all of them several degrees colder than their neighbours, which is the signature of thin cloud or a cloud edge that the cloud mask missed. Three of the six passed the quality flag.

The lesson generalises. A product's quality flags are the first filter, not the last. A robust check against the series' own context (a moving median and MAD, not a mean and standard deviation, which the outliers themselves would distort) catches what the flags miss. And always look at the plot: the cold dots are obvious to the eye long before any rule is written.

::: {.callout-tip}
## A checklist before any graph leaves your desk
- Can someone who has not read the text say what it shows?
- Does the title state a finding, not a topic?
- Are units on every axis, and does the source appear?
- Is the variation visible, or hidden behind an average?
- Would one colour, one highlight and grey everything else say it better?
- For bars: does the axis start at zero?
:::

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Pick any chart from a report you wrote last year. Apply the checklist and redraw it.
2. Redo Rule 2 for Ambon. What does the band show that the average hid?
3. Make the correlation matrix with the season left in. Why does almost everything become strongly correlated?
4. Repeat the ENSO comparison with the Niño 3.4 anomaly of May-June instead of July-October. How much of the relationship survives as a forecast?
5. Apply the moving-median rule to the whole of 2019-2024 for the same Bandung pixel. Do the outliers cluster in particular months?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Answers

**1.** Go through the five rules in order. Common fixes: replace a bar of means with points or a box per group (rule 1); add the range or a band of individual years (rule 2); start bar axes at zero (rule 3); reduce colours to grey context plus one highlight (rule 4); rewrite the title to state the finding and add units and source (rule 5). The test of the redraw: can someone read the main point without your text?

**2.** Not computed in the chapter. Ambon's band of individual years is wide, and its mean shape hides two things: the wet season (around May-August, the opposite of western Indonesia) varies by hundreds of millimetres between years, and the record contains a step change after 2008 (Chapter [-@sec-dataviz]). The band shows that "a typical year" is a poor description: any given year can be far from the average curve.

**3.** With the season left in, every city has a strong annual cycle driven by the same monsoon, so months with high rain in one city tend to have high or low rain in another simply because of the calendar. Correlations become strongly positive (or negative, for cities with opposite regimes) almost everywhere. Removing the season first leaves anomalies, which show whether cities share the unusual months, the question that matters.

**4.** Not computed in the chapter. Correlate July-October rainfall with the May-June Niño 3.4 anomaly. ENSO events usually build through the boreal summer, so the relationship weakens but much of it typically survives: a negative rank correlation, smaller in magnitude than the same-month values (−0.60 to −0.82). How much survives is the forecastable part, the only part useful for planning planting or water releases.

**5.** Not computed in the chapter. Apply the moving-median rule to 2019-2024 and tabulate flagged values by month. If they cluster in the wet season months, they are likely cloud-contaminated observations that passed screening (cold, low LST values in the land surface temperature series); if they cluster in the dry season, look for fire or bare-soil heating. A cluster tells you a process, a scatter tells you noise.
:::
